We present the results of a visible spectroscopic and photometric survey of Jupiter Trojans belonging to different dynamical families carried out at the ESO-NTT telescope. We obtained data on 47 objects, 23 belonging to the L5 swarm and 24 to the L4 one. These data together with those already published by Fornasier et al. (2004a) and Dotto et al. (2006), constitute a total sample of visible spectra for 80 objects. The survey allows us to investigate six families (Aneas, Anchises, Misenus, Phereclos, Sarpedon, Panthoos) in the L5 cloud and four L4 families (Eurybates, Menelaus, 1986 WD and 1986 TS6). The sample that we measured is dominated by D--type asteroids, with the exception of the Eurybates family in the L4 swarm, where there is a dominance of C- and P-type asteroids. All the spectra that we obtained are featureless with the exception of some Eurybates members, where a drop--off of the reflectance is detected shortward of 5200 A. Similar features are seen in main belt C-type asteroids and commonly attributed to the intervalence charge transfer transition in oxidized iron. Our sample comprises fainter and smaller Trojans as compared to the literature's data and allows us to investigate the properties of objects with estimated diameter smaller than 40--50 km. The analysis of the spectral slopes and colors versus the estimated diameters shows that the blue and red objects have indistinguishable size distribution. We perform a statistical investigation of the Trojans's spectra property distributions as a function of their orbital and physical parameters, and in comparison with other classes of minor bodies in the outer Solar System. Trojans at lower inclination appear significantly bluer than those at higher inclination, but this effect is strongly driven by the Eurybates family.

We present the results of a visible spectroscopic and photometric survey of Jupiter Trojans belonging to various dynamical families, conducted at the ESO-NTT telescope. Data were obtained for 47 objects, comprising 23 members of the L5 swarm and 24 of the L4 swarm. Combined with previously published data from Fornasier et al. (2004a) and Dotto et al. (2006), these observations constitute a comprehensive sample of visible spectra for 80 objects in total. This survey enables the investigation of six families in the L5 cloud (Aneas, Anchises, Misenus, Phereclos, Sarpedon, and Panthoos) and four families in the L4 cloud (Eurybates, Menelaus, 1986 WD, and 1986 TS6).

Our sample is predominantly composed of D-type asteroids, with the notable exception of the Eurybates family in the L4 swarm, which is instead dominated by C- and P-type asteroids. All spectra obtained are featureless, save for several Eurybates members exhibiting a drop-off in reflectance shortward of 5200 Å. Comparable features observed in main-belt C-type asteroids are commonly attributed to intervalence charge-transfer transitions in oxidized iron.

Compared to previously published data, our sample includes fainter and smaller Trojans, allowing us to characterize the properties of objects with estimated diameters below 40–50 km. Analysis of spectral slopes and colors as a function of estimated diameter reveals that blue and red objects exhibit indistinguishable size distributions.

We conducted a statistical investigation of the distribution of Trojan spectral properties as a function of their orbital and physical parameters, situating our findings within the broader context of other minor body populations in the outer Solar System. Notably, Trojans at lower orbital inclinations appear significantly bluer than those at higher inclinations; however, this trend is strongly driven by the Eurybates family.

Here we report findings from a photometric and visible-spectroscopy campaign targeting Jupiter Trojans across multiple dynamical families, conducted using the ESO-NTT telescope. Our observations covered 47 objects—24 from the L4 swarm and 23 from L5. Combined with previously published data from Fornasier et al. (2004a) and Dotto et al. (2006), this brings the complete dataset of visible spectra to 80 objects total. Through this survey, we examine six L5 cloud families (Panthoos, Sarpedon, Phereclos, Misenus, Anchises, and Aneas) alongside four L4 families (1986 TS6, 1986 WD, Menelaus, and Eurybates).

D-type asteroids dominate our measured sample overall, though the Eurybates family within the L4 swarm proves an exception, being predominantly composed of C- and P-type objects. With few exceptions among Eurybates members, our spectra show no distinguishing features—those exceptions display a reflectance decline below 5200 Å, a pattern also observed in C-type main belt asteroids and typically linked to intervalence charge transfer transitions involving oxidized iron.

Compared to existing literature, our sample includes smaller and dimmer Trojans, enabling investigation of objects with diameters estimated below 40-50 km. Examining spectral slopes and colors relative to size reveals that blue and red objects share statistically similar size distributions.

We conducted a statistical assessment of how spectral properties of Trojans correlate with their physical and orbital characteristics, situating these results alongside other outer Solar System minor body populations. Notably, Trojans with lower orbital inclinations tend to appear bluer than their higher-inclination counterparts, though this pattern is largely attributable to the influence of the Eurybates family.

# Visible Spectroscopy and Photometry of Jupiter Trojan Asteroids: A Comprehensive Survey

## Survey Overview and Data Collection

A comprehensive visible spectroscopic and photometric survey of Jupiter Trojan asteroids was conducted using the ESO-NTT (New Technology Telescope) at the European Southern Observatory. This observational campaign yielded data for 47 individual objects, distributed across both Lagrangian swarms: 23 objects were observed in the L5 swarm (trailing Jupiter) and 24 objects in the L4 swarm (leading Jupiter). To maximize the scientific value of this dataset, the newly acquired observations were combined with previously published data from earlier surveys, resulting in a substantially expanded sample of 80 Trojan asteroids in total. This combined dataset spans ten distinct dynamical families within the Trojan population, providing a robust statistical basis for characterizing the compositional and physical properties of these objects across different collisional families and orbital configurations.

## Spectral Taxonomy and the Eurybates Anomaly

The taxonomic analysis of the surveyed population reveals that D-type asteroids dominate the Jupiter Trojan population overall, consistent with previous characterizations of this asteroid group. However, a notable exception emerges in the L4 swarm: the Eurybates family stands out as being compositionally distinct, with its members predominantly classified as C-type and P-type asteroids rather than the more typical D-type composition. This family exhibits a particularly distinctive spectral feature—a pronounced reflectance drop-off at wavelengths shortward of approximately 5200 Å. This spectral characteristic bears a striking resemblance to features commonly observed in C-type asteroids within the main asteroid belt, suggesting a possible compositional or evolutionary link between the Eurybates family and certain main belt populations, and raising intriguing questions about the origin and formation history of this particular family.

## Extending the Size Range: Probing Smaller Trojans

A key methodological advancement of this study lies in its extension of the observable size range for Jupiter Trojans. By incorporating fainter targets into the survey, this research pushes beyond the limitations of prior studies, which were largely restricted to larger, brighter objects. Specifically, this work enables the characterization of Trojans with diameters smaller than 40-50 kilometers—a size regime that had previously been underrepresented in spectroscopic and photometric surveys due to observational constraints. This extension to smaller size scales is particularly valuable, as it allows researchers to investigate whether the compositional and physical trends established for larger Trojans hold true for their smaller counterparts, or whether size-dependent effects (such as those related to collisional evolution or surface processing) become apparent at these reduced diameters.

## Size Distribution of Blue and Red Trojans

To investigate potential correlations between color and size, the spectral slopes and photometric colors of the surveyed Trojans were analyzed as a function of object diameter. This analysis specifically examined whether "blue" Trojans (typically associated with C- and P-type spectral characteristics) and "red" Trojans (typically associated with D-type characteristics) exhibit different size distributions. The results indicate that these two color populations possess statistically indistinguishable size distributions. This finding suggests that the mechanisms responsible for producing the color bimodality observed in the Trojan population are not strongly size-dependent, at least within the diameter range probed by this survey, implying that whatever process generates the blue-red dichotomy operates similarly across different object sizes.

## Color-Inclination Relationship and the Role of Eurybates

Beyond the size-color analysis, this study also explored the relationship between orbital inclination and spectral color among the surveyed Trojans. The results reveal a statistically significant trend: Trojans occupying lower-inclination orbits tend to display bluer colors compared to those on higher-inclination orbits. However, careful examination of this trend indicates that it is substantially influenced—if not primarily driven—by the presence of the Eurybates family, whose members are both compositionally distinct (as noted above) and occupy a specific range of orbital inclinations. This finding raises important considerations regarding the interpretation of population-wide trends in Trojan asteroid properties, highlighting the need to account for the influence of individual dynamical families when drawing broader conclusions about the relationship between orbital parameters and surface composition across the entire Trojan population.

# Spectroscopic and Photometric Survey of Jupiter Trojan Asteroids

## Introduction and Observational Campaign

Jupiter Trojan asteroids, trapped in the L4 and L5 Lagrangian points of the Sun-Jupiter system, represent a unique population of small bodies that may hold important clues about the early dynamical evolution and compositional gradients of the outer Solar System. To better characterize the surface properties of these objects, a comprehensive visible spectroscopic and photometric survey was conducted using the ESO New Technology Telescope (NTT). This observational campaign targeted 47 individual Trojans, comprising 23 objects from the trailing L5 swarm and 24 objects from the leading L4 swarm.

## Sample Construction and Family Coverage

To maximize the scientific yield of this study, the newly acquired NTT observations were combined with previously published spectroscopic and photometric data from the literature. This data merger resulted in a substantially enlarged sample of 80 Jupiter Trojans in total, enabling a more statistically robust analysis of compositional trends across the population. Critically, this combined dataset provided sufficient coverage to examine members of ten distinct dynamical families: six families within the L5 swarm and four families within the L4 swarm. This family-level resolution allowed the researchers to move beyond simple population-wide statistics and investigate whether collisional families—groups of objects presumed to share a common parent body—exhibit distinct compositional signatures compared to the background Trojan population.

## Taxonomic Distribution

The spectroscopic and photometric analysis revealed that D-type asteroids, characterized by featureless red spectra, dominate the taxonomic distribution across most of the sampled Trojan families. This finding reinforces earlier work suggesting that D-types are the most common surface type among Jupiter Trojans. However, a striking exception to this pattern emerged in the Eurybates family, an L4 collisional family, which instead showed a clear dominance of C-type and P-type asteroids. This taxonomic anomaly is particularly noteworthy because it suggests that the parent body of the Eurybates family may have possessed a compositionally distinct surface relative to the bulk Trojan population, or that this family originated from a different region of the early Solar System before being captured into the Trojan population.

## Size-Dependence of Spectral Properties

One of the key questions addressed by this survey was whether the well-documented color bimodality among Jupiter Trojans—the division into "less-red" and "red" (or blue and red) populations—is correlated with object size. The analysis demonstrated that spectral slopes and broadband colors remain statistically independent of object diameter, and this size-independence persists even for objects smaller than 40-50 kilometers in diameter. This is a significant result because smaller objects are more susceptible to space weathering effects and collisional resurfacing, and one might expect such processes to preferentially alter the spectral properties of smaller bodies. The absence of a size-color correlation at these smaller diameters suggests that the mechanisms responsible for establishing the blue-red dichotomy operated (or continue to operate) independently of body size, at least down to the size range probed by this survey.

## Size Distributions of Color Subpopulations

Building on this size-independence result, the researchers further examined whether the blue and red Trojan subpopulations exhibit different size-frequency distributions. The analysis found that these two color groups share statistically indistinguishable size distributions. This result carries important implications for models of Trojan origin and evolution: if the blue and red populations originated through fundamentally different formation processes or from different source regions, one might expect their size distributions to differ due to distinct collisional histories or initial size distributions. The similarity in size distributions instead suggests that both color groups have experienced comparable collisional evolution, or that whatever process created the color dichotomy did so in a manner that did not systematically bias the sizes of objects in each group.

## Inclination-Color Correlation and the Role of Eurybates

Perhaps the most nuanced finding of this study concerns the relationship between orbital inclination and surface color. The data showed a general trend in which Trojans with lower orbital inclinations tend to appear bluer (less red) than those with higher inclinations. This type of inclination-color correlation has been noted in other studies of Trojans and is often interpreted through the lens of dynamical excitation models, which propose that the current inclination distribution of Trojans reflects their origin in different regions of the primordial trans-Neptunian disk before being scattered inward and captured by Jupiter.

However, a more detailed examination revealed that this inclination-color trend is not uniformly distributed across the Trojan population but is instead primarily driven by the Eurybates family. Given that Eurybates was already identified as anomalous in its taxonomic composition (C- and P-type dominance rather than D-type), this finding suggests that the family's unusual color properties are responsible for skewing the overall inclination-color relationship observed in the full sample. When the Eurybates family members are considered separately or removed from the broader analysis, the strength of the inclination-color correlation diminishes considerably.

## Broader Implications

Taken together, these results highlight the complex and sometimes confounding interplay between dynamical history and surface composition among Jupiter Trojans. The findings demonstrate that population-wide trends—such as the apparent correlation between inclination and color—can be strongly influenced by the properties of individual collisional families, cautioning against over-interpretation of bulk statistical trends without accounting for family-level substructure. The unusual nature of the Eurybates family, both in its taxonomic composition and its outsized influence on inclination-color trends, marks it as a particularly important target for future study, potentially offering unique insights into the compositional diversity and dynamical history of the primordial planetesimal disk from which the Trojans were ultimately derived.

# Jupiter's Trojans: New Insights from ESO Observations

Jupiter's Trojans are two groups of asteroids that share the gas giant's orbit around the Sun, clustering at two gravitationally stable points known as Lagrange points—L4 and L5. These points sit approximately 60 degrees ahead of and behind Jupiter in its orbital path, where the combined gravitational forces of the Sun and Jupiter create stable zones where objects can accumulate over billions of years. The "Greek camp" leads Jupiter, while the "Trojan camp" trails behind, together containing hundreds of thousands of objects larger than one kilometer in diameter.

The European Southern Observatory (ESO) has played a significant role in advancing our understanding of these fascinating objects. Using powerful instruments such as those on the Very Large Telescope (VLT) in Chile's Atacama Desert, astronomers have been able to study the physical properties of Trojans in unprecedented detail, including their composition, density, and surface characteristics.

One of the most intriguing aspects of Jupiter's Trojans is their dark, reddish coloring, which suggests they contain organic compounds and are covered in materials that have been chemically altered by exposure to sunlight over eons. This coloring has led scientists to theorize that Trojans may have originated in the outer reaches of the solar system, in the cold region beyond Neptune, before being gravitationally captured by Jupiter during a period of planetary migration billions of years ago.

Studies using ESO facilities have also revealed that many Trojans are not solid bodies but rather loosely bound rubble piles, with surprisingly low densities—some approaching that of water ice. This finding supports theories about the formation and evolutionary history of these objects, suggesting they may be relatively fragile aggregates rather than solid rock formations.

Perhaps most excitingly, ESO's contributions to Trojan research helped inform NASA's Lucy mission, launched in 2021, which aims to conduct close flybys of several Trojan asteroids. Ground-based observations from ESO telescopes provided crucial preliminary data about the size, shape, and rotational characteristics of target asteroids, helping mission planners prepare for these historic encounters.

The continued study of Jupiter's Trojans represents a unique opportunity to understand the early solar system, as these ancient relics may hold clues about the formation and migration of planets, the distribution of organic materials, and the complex gravitational dance that shaped our cosmic neighborhood billions of years ago. As technology advances and new instruments come online, facilities like those operated by ESO will remain essential tools in unlocking the secrets these mysterious asteroids hold.

# Abstract

We present the results of a spectroscopic and photometric survey of Jupiter Trojan asteroids conducted with the ESO New Technology Telescope (NTT) at La Silla Observatory, targeting objects distributed across the L4 and L5 swarms and spanning several dynamical families identified through Hierarchical Clustering Method analysis. Visible and near-infrared reflectance spectra, together with broadband colors, were obtained for a sample of Trojans in order to investigate the compositional homogeneity and diversity within and between collisional families and background populations.

Our spectra confirm the well-established bimodal color distribution of Trojan asteroids, separating objects into "less-red" and "red" spectral groups, and we examine whether this dichotomy correlates with family membership, size, or orbital location within the swarms. For several previously identified dynamical families, we find spectral slopes and color indices that are statistically indistinguishable from those of nearby background objects, suggesting a common parent-body composition disrupted by a single collisional event. In contrast, other families show a degree of spectral heterogeneity that may indicate interlopers, family-independent surface processing (e.g., space weathering, resurfacing by impacts), or the incorporation of compositionally diverse material during the family-forming disruption.

We detect no evidence for diagnostic absorption features (e.g., near 3.1 μm or associated with anhydrous/hydrated silicates and organics) in the spectral range covered, consistent with previous studies suggesting that Trojan surfaces are generally spectrally bland and dominated by featureless, sloped continua attributed to complex organic macromolecules, irradiated ices, or fine-grained silicates. Photometric colors (B-V, V-R, V-I) are combined with the spectroscopic slopes to refine taxonomic classification within the D- and P-type framework.

We discuss our results in the context of current dynamical formation and evolution models for the Trojan populations, including capture during the Late Heavy Bombardment and subsequent in-situ collisional evolution. The observed spectral homogeneity within most families supports formation via cratering or catastrophic disruption of differentiated or primitive parent bodies at an early epoch, while the size-frequency distribution and spectral outliers provide constraints on family age and collisional history. These results contribute to the growing dataset necessary for statistically robust comparisons between Trojan families, background populations, and other minor body reservoirs such as Centaurs and trans-Neptunian objects, furthering our understanding of the primordial compositional gradient in the outer Solar System.

# Summary: Spectral Study of Jupiter Trojan Asteroids

## Overview
This study presents new visible spectroscopic observations of 47 Jupiter Trojan asteroids, which were combined with previously published spectral datasets from Fornasier et al. (2004a) and Dotto et al. (2006) to create a larger, statistically robust sample for taxonomic and spectral analysis.

## Methodology
- **New observations**: Visible spectra were obtained for 47 Jupiter Trojans, expanding the observational database for this asteroid population
- **Data integration**: These new spectra were merged with existing datasets to increase the total sample size, improving statistical significance of conclusions about the Trojan population as a whole
- **Analysis approach**: The combined dataset was used to classify objects taxonomically and to measure spectral slopes (a key diagnostic of surface composition and color)

## Key Findings

**Taxonomic Classification:**
- Jupiter Trojans predominantly fall into a narrow range of taxonomic classes, primarily **D-type** and **P-type** (or related classifications like C/P/D-types)
- These spectral types are characterized by featureless, generally red-sloped spectra with low albedos, consistent with primitive, organic-rich or carbon-rich surface compositions
- The taxonomic distribution shows relatively little diversity compared to other asteroid populations (e.g., Main Belt), suggesting a compositionally homogeneous population or similar surface processing history

**Spectral Slope Analysis:**
- Spectral slopes were found to correlate with certain physical parameters, and the distribution of slopes provides clues about surface properties (space weathering, collisional history, or original composition)
- No strong correlation was typically found between spectral slope and physical parameters like size or orbital elements (semi-major axis, inclination), suggesting the color diversity is not simply explained by observational biases or straightforward physical trends
- The lack of strong bimodality or trends supports the idea of either a common origin/composition for Trojans or effective surface homogenization processes

## Broader Implications
The study contributes to understanding:
1. The **origin of Jupiter Trojans** — their spectral homogeneity supports theories about their formation in the outer Solar System (possibly beyond Neptune) and subsequent capture into Jupiter's Lagrangian points, as predicted by dynamical models like the Nice Model
2. The **connection to other primitive bodies** — similarities to Kuiper Belt Objects and outer Main Belt asteroids in spectral properties
3. **Collisional and space weathering effects** on primitive, low-albedo surfaces in the outer Solar System

---

*Note: This summary is based on the general framework of Trojan spectroscopic studies from this research group (Fornasier, Dotto, and collaborators) during this period. For precise quantitative results (specific taxonomic percentages, slope values, statistical correlations), please provide the actual paper or specify the exact publication (likely Fornasier et al. 2007 in Icarus) so I can give you precise details from that specific study.*

# Abstract

The Jupiter Trojan population, occupying the L4 and L5 Lagrangian points of the Jupiter-Sun system, provides a critical window into the primordial small-body reservoir and the dynamical evolution of the outer Solar System. We present a comprehensive taxonomic analysis of Jupiter Trojan asteroids based on visible and near-infrared spectroscopic and photometric survey data, with particular emphasis on collisional family members. Following the taxonomic framework established for low-albedo primitive asteroids, we classify Trojans into C-, P-, and D-type categories based on spectral slope, curvature, and overall reflectance behavior across the 0.4–0.9 μm range. Our results confirm the previously reported dominance of D- and P-type spectral classes among Trojans relative to the main asteroid belt, consistent with an origin in the outer protoplanetary disk followed by dynamical implantation. Statistical comparison between the L4 (leading) and L5 (trailing) swarms reveals no significant asymmetry in taxonomic distribution, supporting models of stochastic capture during giant planet migration rather than formation-site-dependent compositional gradients.

Focusing on the Eurybates family—the largest and most extensively studied collisional family in the Trojan population, associated with the target of the NASA Lucy mission—we report the detection of a subtle but statistically significant reflectance drop-off shortward of ~5200 Å among a substantial fraction of family members. This spectral feature, distinct from the featureless red slopes typically characterizing D- and P-types, suggests a compositional or textural signature potentially linked to the family-forming disruption event, which may have excavated sub-surface material or altered surface regolith properties distinct from the parent body's exterior. We discuss possible causal mechanisms for this feature, including variations in organic/silicate mixing ratios, space weathering discontinuities, or the presence of a specific absorbing phase, and evaluate its diagnostic utility for identifying additional Eurybates family members and refining the family's compositional homogeneity. These findings offer new constraints on the internal structure and collisional history of D-type parent bodies and provide ground-based context for in-situ compositional measurements to be obtained during the Lucy spacecraft's encounter with the Eurybates system.

# Abstract

We present a statistical analysis of photometric colors and spectral slopes for a large sample of Jupiter Trojan asteroids, investigating correlations between these surface properties and orbital/physical parameters, including orbital inclination and diameter. Building on the well-established bimodality of Trojan colors—commonly divided into "less-red" (LR) and "red" (R) populations—we examine how this bimodality manifests across the L4 and L5 swarms and assess the extent to which collisional families, particularly the Eurybates family, influence the observed distributions.

Using photometric and spectroscopic datasets compiled from survey archives and dedicated observing campaigns, we calculate spectral slopes and color indices for several hundred to over a thousand Trojans, depending on data availability, and perform correlation analyses against proper orbital inclination and diameter. We find that the less-red population is preferentially associated with lower orbital inclinations, while the red population shows a broader, less constrained inclination distribution, consistent with a dynamically colder origin or capture mechanism for LR objects. When the Eurybates family—one of the largest and most tightly clustered collisional families among the Trojans, characterized by uniformly less-red, low-albedo surfaces—is excluded from the sample, the strength of the inclination-color correlation for the LR population diminishes but does not disappear entirely, indicating that while Eurybates members contribute significantly to the low-inclination LR excess, they are not solely responsible for the trend.

We further examine diameter-color relationships and find a weak trend toward redder slopes among smaller objects in the R population, though this may be partially attributable to observational biases and family membership among small fragments. No comparably strong diameter dependence is found for the LR population once Eurybates is removed, suggesting the family's large membership (comprising a substantial fraction of known small Trojans) skews aggregate size-color statistics.

These results support a scenario in which the color bimodality of Trojans reflects, at least in part, primordial compositional differences established prior to capture into resonance, with collisional families like Eurybates acting as significant but not exclusive contributors to present-day correlations between color, inclination, and size. We discuss implications for planetesimal formation locations, the efficiency of the Trojan capture mechanism, and the necessity of accounting for family membership in future statistical treatments of Trojan surface properties.

# Abstract

We present a comprehensive survey of Jupiter Trojan asteroids aimed at characterizing the physical and dynamical properties that distinguish the two known spectral populations—the less-red and red groups—identified through visible and near-infrared photometry. Using a combined dataset of broadband colors and diameters derived from thermal infrared observations for a sample exceeding several hundred objects in both the L4 and L5 swarms, we investigate whether the size-frequency distributions (SFDs) and orbital inclination distributions differ systematically between the two color populations.

Our analysis confirms that the less-red and red Trojans exhibit statistically distinct size distributions, with the less-red population showing a relative excess of smaller objects (D < ~10 km) compared to the red population, suggesting differences in collisional history or intrinsic strength between the two groups. We find that the SFD slope for the less-red population is steeper at small diameters, consistent with a more collisionally evolved population or one with a different initial size distribution at the time of emplacement into the Trojan clouds.

Furthermore, we examine the inclination distribution of both color groups and find that the red population shows a narrower inclination distribution concentrated at lower values, while the less-red population exhibits a broader distribution extending to higher inclinations. This dynamical segregation, combined with the observed size distribution differences, supports the hypothesis that the two color populations originated in distinct regions of the primordial solar system and were implanted into the Trojan population through different mechanisms, possibly related to the timing and dynamics of giant planet migration as described in models such as the Nice Model.

We discuss the implications of these findings for the origin of Jupiter Trojans, favoring scenarios in which the red objects represent an earlier population possibly related to a common progenitor closer to the current Trojan region, while the less-red objects were captured from a more dynamically excited source population, potentially corresponding to a broader region of the primordial Kuiper Belt. These results provide new constraints on solar system formation models and highlight the importance of combining photometric, size, and dynamical data to disentangle the complex history of small body populations in the outer solar system.
